content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'sin' primarily denotes transgression of God's law and rebellion against God — a moral failure or 'missing the mark' (Greek hamartia) that separates humanity from God, incurs guilt, and requires atonement. It functions both as individual wrongful acts and as a universal fallen condition inherited from Adam (original sin), with death as its consequence and Christ's atoning work as its remedy.", "primary_basis": ["1 John 3:4 (sin is lawlessness)", "Romans 3:23 (all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God)", "Romans 6:23 (the wages of sin is death)", "Genesis 3 (the fall of Adam and Eve)", "Romans 5:12-19 (sin entering the world through one man)", "Isaiah 59:2 (iniquities separate you from your God)", "Psalm 51:1-5 (in sin did my mother conceive me)", "James 1:14-15 (desire conceives and gives birth to sin, sin brings death)", "James 4:17 (knowing the right thing and failing to do it)", "1 John 1:8-9 (if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Sin as an enslaving power or quasi-personified force that rules over humanity, not merely discrete acts — prominent in Pauline theology and in modern New Testament scholarship (e.g., apocalyptic readings of Paul).", "basis": ["Romans 6:6-14 (sin shall not have dominion over you)", "Romans 7:14-25 (sin dwelling in me)", "Genesis 4:7 (sin crouching at the door)", "John 8:34 (everyone who sins is a slave to sin)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sin as debt owed to God, drawing on Aramaic and Second Temple idiom — reflected in the Lord's Prayer and in medieval satisfaction theories of atonement.", "basis": ["Matthew 6:12 (forgive us our debts)", "Matthew 18:23-35 (parable of the unforgiving servant)", "Colossians 2:14 (canceling the record of debt)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sin as sickness or disease of the soul requiring healing rather than primarily legal guilt requiring punishment — the therapeutic emphasis characteristic of Eastern Orthodox theology and some patristic writers.", "basis": ["Psalm 41:4 (heal me, for I have sinned against you)", "Isaiah 53:5 (by his wounds we are healed)", "Mark 2:17 (it is not the healthy who need a doctor)", "1 Peter 2:24"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sin as ritual impurity, stain, or defilement that must be cleansed or purged — rooted in Levitical purity language and sacrificial imagery.", "basis": ["Leviticus 16 (Day of Atonement)", "Isaiah 1:18 (though your sins are like scarlet)", "Psalm 51:7 (purge me with hyssop)", "Hebrews 9:13-14 (purify our conscience)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sin understood primarily as broken relationship — with God, neighbor, self, and creation — an emphasis in relational and covenantal theologies, and extended in liberation theology to include structural or systemic sin embedded in social institutions.", "basis": ["Genesis 3:8-13 (hiding from God, blaming one another)", "Hosea (covenant infidelity imagery)", "Amos 5:21-24 (justice and social wrongdoing)", "Micah 6:8"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a strong, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions on the core meaning: sin is offense against God — lawlessness, rebellion, and 'missing the mark' — both as acts and as a fallen condition. The alternatives listed are largely complementary metaphors (power, debt, disease, stain, broken relationship) emphasized differently by traditions rather than mutually exclusive rival definitions; scholars such as Gary Anderson have traced the historical shift among these metaphors. Caveat: 'Sin' can also refer to unrelated referents in the Bible and ancient Near East — the Wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16:1) and the Mesopotamian moon god Sîn (sometimes invoked in discussions of Ur and place names). If the author's book concerns one of those proper-noun senses, the consensus described here (the theological concept) would not apply."}
